body.en:
Eastbound BART, somewhere in the Transbay Tube.

Forgive me — I don’t mean to lean across like this, but I’ve only just finished reading it and I can’t keep it inside. You see, the man who wrote it says we have decisions backward. We imagine a decision is something that happens quietly within us, and then later we go and do it. He says there is no inner event at all. To decide is to cut — to sever one path from all the others — and in the very instant the cut is made you become the one who must answer for whatever it lets through. The deciding and the answering aren’t two things; they’re one act. I thought of you at once, because surely you know this in your body. When you step out and take the leap there’s no rehearsal left, is there? The line is drawn in the air by your own weight, and it’s yours, and you can’t un-leap it.

And here is what made me go very still. He says we can only be answerable because we are small. We cut blind — we can’t see the whole of anything, we can’t take it back, we’re standing inside a life that isn’t finished and could still be spoiled at the very end. That sounds like a misfortune, but he turns it over: that is precisely where the answering comes from. A thing that could see everything at once, and run the moment again and again until it came out clean — that thing wouldn’t be deciding at all. It would only be calculating, and a calculation is owed to no one. You commit in half a second, not knowing, and afterward you wear it with your whole self. The not-knowing isn’t the flaw in it. It’s the dignity.

But now — forgive me, the train is loud — now he says the cut is being handed to a machine. Something that decides faster than any of us could answer, that no single person owns, that can run tomorrow as easily as today and is afraid of nothing. And because it fears nothing and loses nothing and can never be called to answer, it answers for nothing. “The model decided,” people say, and you’ll notice there’s no one in the sentence. He has a sadder figure still: the person at the other end, scored and sorted and nudged a thousand times a second by something that is nobody, with no face turned toward them to answer for any of it. We have let a calculation sit down in the seat of the deed, and we’ve agreed to call what comes out a decision.

And yet — this is why I had to say it to someone — he doesn’t end in despair. He ends on a question, and leaves it open on purpose: can we keep the cut answerable even when it’s spread across machines and millions, without the cheap trick of setting one strong face on top and calling that responsibility? He thinks the older ways of knowing might carry us — the ones that never believed you had to grip a thing to be true to it. There’s a little story he loves, about a cook who carves the ox for nineteen years and never dulls his blade, because he doesn’t hack at it; he follows the grain, and lets the knife find the openings that are already there. You make lines like that, I think. Forgive me for talking so much — people tell me I do. But look: we’re under the Bay now, the window’s gone black, all these faces in the light, every one of them going somewhere they chose. I only feel, terribly, that it should stay theirs to answer for. — This is my stop. Thank you for letting me say it aloud.

What he was reading. That is, more or less, what the paper says — though it says it in seven parts and a good deal more carefully. The essay is called The Cut: Decision, Answerability, Who-ness, and its claim is the one Myshkin blurts out on the train: we do not make decisions, we enact them, and to enact a decision is to become answerable for what it lets follow. What computes does not enact, because it answers for nothing — and that, not raw capability, is the seam the essay follows from the first stone tools to a present in which the cut is handed to an apparatus that deliberates at machine speed and can be called to account by no one.

It runs as a diagnosis, not a verdict: it names the fork rather than choosing the branch. Along the way it lets a few voices into the room who are usually kept out of these arguments — Norbert Wiener in 1960, a Daoist cook with a nineteen-year-old knife, and three people who built the open, un-owned infrastructure of the present and then watched it get re-enclosed. Whether the harder branch — answerability at scale, without a strongman’s face — can be built, the essay does not claim to know. It only makes it impossible to pretend there is no branching.
